Darreggio is the mirn—the masculine form—of mechanics, or, as the exhibition puts it, engineering. He is the patron of mechanics, in keeping with the location of his temple in the craftsmen’s square.

On the academy clock (ch. 5)

On the tower of the Academy of Arts, Darreggio’s figurine emerges beneath an enameled sun at three in the afternoon, replacing Vinsenya. The narrator ironically calls him a lazy fellow.

Darreggio in a painting (ch. 16)

At the “Philosophy of Horror” exhibition in the Eliste Gallery, one painting shows Darreggio cutting open his own belly and inserting a miniature steam engine. His extracted intestines lie beside him, with flies circling above them. The caption reads: “The highest power is power over oneself.” Filippe di Berro advises Alvaro to think about it.

The temple in Craftsmen’s Square (ch. 30)

A grey-stone temple of Darreggio stands at the center of Laerta’s Craftsmen’s Square. It forces the flow of people around the edges of the square. Two-story houses crowd its perimeter, each containing a workshop or shop: a shoemaker’s, a hardware shop, or a coppersmith’s. The narrator says that the square recalls a time when the city was sustained by small family workshops, without monopolies.
